## The measure is chosen before any model is fitted

[Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd) and
[Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd) showed that measures can
rank the same models in different orders. So the measure should be chosen before any model is
fitted, from what the predictions will be used for. A map of abundance, a stock total, a list
of stations to revisit and a decision at each station ask different things of a model, and a
model that is best at one can be poor at another. This page sets out which measure suits
which use, and adds two the earlier pages did not cover: the catch found by a shortlist, and
the cost of the calls at a threshold chosen from what each mistake costs.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Each use has its own measure

| The predictions are used for | Score them with |
| --- | --- |
| A map of abundance | the RMSE, aimed at the average count, and R² as `rsq_trad()` or `r2_score()` |
| A total, such as a stock estimate | the predicted total over the observed one, beside the RMSE |
| The typical station, where totals do not matter | MAE, aimed at the median |
| A shortlist of the most promising stations | the animals the shortlist finds, against a perfect and a random shortlist |
| A map of the chance of presence | log loss, with a calibration plot |
| Comparing models before a threshold is chosen | ROC AUC |
| A call at each station | the expected cost of the calls, at a threshold chosen from the costs; balanced accuracy or MCC while the costs are unknown |

[Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd) and
[Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd) showed why the first
rows and the map of chances need their measures; this page adds the shortlist and the call
at each station. A total alone is never enough: predicting the average gets the total
right and says nothing about any station. None of these measures says whether an input causes what it predicts, which
[Linearity and nonlinearity](../06-assumptions-limitations/linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd)
showed a good predictor need not do.

## A shortlist is scored on what it finds

Suppose a ship has time to revisit a fixed number of stations, its **budget**, and goes to
the ones a model predicts the most animals at: a **shortlist**. The measure is the number of animals caught
at those stations. Two benchmarks make it readable: a **perfect shortlist**, the stations
that really held the most, and a random one, which finds the budget times the average catch.

The shortlist depends only on the order of the predictions. Halving every prediction
changes the RMSE and leaves the shortlist exactly as it was, so a model whose predictions
run low, which the RMSE and R² punish, loses nothing here as long as it puts the stations in
the right order. This is the same property as ROC AUC for presence, applied to a fixed number
of stations.

## The costs of the two mistakes set the threshold

[Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd#a-threshold-set-from-the-costs-does-the-work-of-rebalancing)
said that the threshold should come from what each mistake costs. This can be made exact
with the two mistakes of [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd#the-threshold-trades-false-alarms-for-misses):
a false alarm, a station called present where the species is absent, and a miss, a station
called absent where it is present. If a false alarm costs $k$ times as much as a miss, the
**expected cost** of the calls is

$$
\text{expected cost} = \frac{\text{misses} + k \times \text{false alarms}}{\text{stations}},
$$

in units of one miss. A model that gives a station probability $p$ of presence expects a
cost of $p$ from calling it absent and $k(1 - p)$ from calling it present. Calling it
present is cheaper when $p$ is above $k/(1+k)$, so that is the threshold. When both mistakes
cost the same, $k = 1$ and the threshold is the familiar 0.5; when a false alarm costs three
times a miss, it is 0.75.

::: {.diagram}
![The threshold from the costs. Left, a false alarm costs three times a miss, and two stations are weighed: at a probability of presence of 0.6, calling it present expects a cost of 1.2 and calling it absent 0.6, so it is called absent; at 0.9, calling it present expects 0.3 and absent 0.9, so it is called present. Right, the threshold k over 1 plus k on the probability scale: 0.5 when the two mistakes cost the same, 0.75 when a false alarm costs three times a miss, 0.83 when it costs five times.](img/cost-threshold.svg){fig-alt="Two cards. Left, a false alarm costs 3 misses: for a station with probability 0.6, a bar for calling it present shows an expected cost of 3 times 0.4, which is 1.2, and a bar for calling it absent shows 0.6, so the cheaper call is absent. For a station with probability 0.9, calling it present costs 3 times 0.1, which is 0.3, and calling it absent costs 0.9, so the cheaper call is present. Right, the threshold is k over 1 plus k: an axis of probability of presence from 0 to 1, with three marks, 0.5 when k is 1, 0.75 when k is 3 and 0.83 when k is 5. Stations above the mark are called present. A note says the rule holds only when the probabilities are calibrated."}
:::

The rule needs calibrated probabilities, as
[Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd#log-loss-rewards-probabilities-that-are-spread-out-and-calibrated)
checked with a calibration plot. If a model's 0.8 does not mean 8 in 10, the cheapest
threshold has to be found by working out the expected cost at every threshold instead.

## Worked example

The shortlist is drawn from three of the models on
[Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd): **linear regression**, the
**random forest**, and the **random forest on log counts**, whose predictions add up to well
below the catch. The calls come from **logistic regression**, from
[Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd), whose probabilities were
calibrated there. All four models are cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites as on
those pages, so their out-of-fold predictions are the same.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |>
  mutate(log_abundance = log1p(abundance))

set.seed(61)
folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10)

inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
            "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude")

with_inputs <- function(outcome, model) {
  recipe(reformulate(inputs, outcome), data = survey) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    workflow(model)
}

forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |>
  set_mode("regression")

log_forest <- "Random forest on log counts"

models <- list(
  "Linear regression"           = with_inputs("abundance", linear_reg()),
  "Random forest"               = with_inputs("abundance", forest),
  "Random forest on log counts" = with_inputs("log_abundance", forest)
)

# every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order
out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) {
  fit_resamples(model, folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse),
                control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |>
    collect_predictions() |>
    arrange(.row) |>
    pull(.pred)
})
# back from log counts to animals
out_of_fold[[log_forest]] <- expm1(out_of_fold[[log_forest]])

caught <- survey$abundance

tibble(stations = nrow(survey),
       `animals caught` = sum(caught),
       `average catch` = round(mean(caught), 2))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()
caught = survey["abundance"].to_numpy()

folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61)

inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
          "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical]

def with_inputs(model):
    recipe = ColumnTransformer([
        # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged and helps the solver
        ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                              ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric),
        ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical),
    ])
    return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)])

# max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does.
forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt",
                               min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=1)

models = {
    "Linear regression": LinearRegression(),
    "Random forest": forest,
    # fitted to log counts, each prediction turned back into animals
    "Random forest on log counts": TransformedTargetRegressor(
        forest, func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1),
}

# every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order
out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], caught,
                                       cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"])
               for name, model in models.items()}

pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "animals caught": [caught.sum()],
              "average catch": [round(caught.mean(), 2)]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| include: false
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
pct <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
```

### Predictions that run low lose nothing on a shortlist

The ship has time for 100 of the `r nrow(survey)` stations. The table sets each model's
shortlist beside its RMSE and its predicted total.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: shortlists
budget <- 100

# the animals caught at the stations a set of predictions ranks highest
found_by <- function(predicted) {
  sum(caught[order(predicted, decreasing = TRUE)][seq_len(budget)])
}

perfect <- sum(sort(caught, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(budget)])
at_random <- budget * mean(caught)

shortlists <- tibble(
  model = names(out_of_fold),
  RMSE = map_dbl(out_of_fold, \(predicted) rmse_vec(caught, predicted)),
  `predicted / caught` = map_dbl(out_of_fold,
                                 \(predicted) sum(predicted) / sum(caught)),
  `animals found` = map_dbl(out_of_fold, found_by),
  `share of a perfect shortlist` = `animals found` / perfect
)

shortlists |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
budget = 100

# the animals caught at the stations a set of predictions ranks highest
def found_by(predicted):
    return caught[np.argsort(-predicted, kind="stable")][:budget].sum()

perfect = np.sort(caught)[::-1][:budget].sum()
at_random = budget * caught.mean()

shortlists = pd.DataFrame([
    {"model": name,
     "RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(caught, predicted),
     "predicted / caught": predicted.sum() / caught.sum(),
     "animals found": found_by(predicted),
     "share of a perfect shortlist": found_by(predicted) / perfect}
    for name, predicted in out_of_fold.items()])

shortlists.round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: shortlist-numbers
#| include: false
list_of <- function(name, measure) shortlists[[measure]][shortlists$model == name]
found_ratio <- mean(shortlists[["animals found"]]) / at_random
```

A perfect shortlist of `r budget` stations would find `r format(perfect, big.mark = ",")` animals, and
`r budget` stations chosen at random about `r round(at_random)`. The forest on log counts
has the highest RMSE of the three, `r f2(list_of(log_forest, "RMSE"))`, and predicts only
`r pct(list_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` of the animals caught. Its shortlist
finds `r list_of(log_forest, "animals found")` animals, against
`r list_of("Random forest", "animals found")` for the same forest fitted to the counts and
`r list_of("Linear regression", "animals found")` for linear regression. Its predictions
run low, but in much the same order, and the order is all a shortlist uses.

The gaps between the three are small. The Python tab, with its own folds and forests, puts
them in another order, and
[Uncertainty and stability](uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) showed that gaps this size need a
paired comparison before they count as a ranking. The result shared by all three is plainer:
each shortlist finds about `r pct(mean(shortlists[["share of a perfect shortlist"]]))` of
what a perfect one would, and `r sprintf("%.1f", found_ratio)` times what a random one
finds. A sentence such as "revisiting the `r budget` stations this model ranks highest
should find about `r sprintf("%.1f", found_ratio)` times as many animals as `r budget`
stations chosen at random" tells a survey planner more than an RMSE does.

### The cheapest threshold follows the cost of a false alarm

Suppose every station called present is visited by a dive team. A false alarm wastes a dive;
a miss leaves a station with the species out of the record. The expected cost is worked out
at every threshold from 0.01 to 0.99, for false alarms that cost one, three and five times as
much as a miss. The last column is the cheaper of two rules that need no model: call every
station present, or call none.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: costs
# logistic regression's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order
probability <- fit_resamples(with_inputs("present", logistic_reg()), folds,
                             metrics = metric_set(roc_auc),
                             control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |>
  collect_predictions() |>
  arrange(.row) |>
  pull(.pred_yes)

present <- survey$present == "yes"

expected_cost <- function(threshold, k) {
  called <- probability >= threshold
  (sum(!called & present) + k * sum(called & !present)) / length(present)
}

cost_curves <- expand_grid(k = c(1, 3, 5), threshold = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(cost = map2_dbl(threshold, k, expected_cost))

cheapest <- cost_curves |>
  slice_min(cost, by = k, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(`k / (1 + k)` = k / (1 + k),
         `stations called present` = map_int(threshold, \(t) sum(probability >= t)),
         `cost at 0.5` = map_dbl(k, \(k) expected_cost(0.5, k)),
         # calling every station present, or none
         `cost without the model` = pmin(k * mean(!present), mean(present))) |>
  select(k, `k / (1 + k)`, `cheapest threshold` = threshold,
         `stations called present`, `cost there` = cost, `cost at 0.5`,
         `cost without the model`)

cheapest |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
# logistic regression's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order;
# column 1 of predict_proba is the probability of True
present = (survey["present"] == "yes").to_numpy()
probability = cross_val_predict(
    with_inputs(LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=5000)), survey[inputs], present,
    cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"], method="predict_proba")[:, 1]

def expected_cost(threshold, k):
    called = probability >= threshold
    return (np.sum(~called & present) + k * np.sum(called & ~present)) / len(present)

thresholds = np.round(np.arange(0.01, 0.995, 0.01), 2)

def cheapest_for(k):
    costs = np.array([expected_cost(t, k) for t in thresholds])
    best = thresholds[np.argmin(costs)]
    return {"k": k, "k / (1 + k)": k / (1 + k), "cheapest threshold": best,
            "stations called present": int(np.sum(probability >= best)),
            "cost there": costs.min(), "cost at 0.5": expected_cost(0.5, k),
            # calling every station present, or none
            "cost without the model": min(k * np.mean(~present), np.mean(present))}

cheapest = pd.DataFrame([cheapest_for(k) for k in (1, 3, 5)])

cheapest.round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: cost-numbers
#| include: false
cost_of <- function(k, column) cheapest[[column]][cheapest$k == k]
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-cost
#| fig-cap: !expr glue::glue("Expected cost of logistic regression's calls at every threshold, in units of one miss, when a false alarm costs one, three and five times as much as a miss. The point marks the cheapest threshold, named above each panel, the dashed line 0.5, and the dotted line the cost without the model. The cheapest threshold moves from {f2(cost_of(1, 'cheapest threshold'))} to {f2(cost_of(5, 'cheapest threshold'))} as false alarms get dearer, close to k/(1 + k) each time.")
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Three panels side by side, for a false alarm costing 1, 3 and 5 misses, each with the threshold from 0 to 1 along the bottom and the expected cost per station up the side, a dashed vertical line at 0.5 and a dotted horizontal line for the cost without the model. Each curve has a marked lowest point, at {f2(cost_of(1, 'cheapest threshold'))} when the two mistakes cost the same, {f2(cost_of(3, 'cheapest threshold'))} when a false alarm costs 3 misses and {f2(cost_of(5, 'cheapest threshold'))} when it costs 5, each a little below the dotted line. In the five-times panel the curve at 0.5 is {f2(cost_of(5, 'cost at 0.5'))}, far above the dotted line at {f2(cost_of(5, 'cost without the model'))}.")
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 3.7
panels <- transmute(cheapest, k, panel = sprintf(
  "A false alarm costs %g %s\ncheapest at %.2f",
  k, if_else(k == 1, "miss", "misses"), `cheapest threshold`))
cost_curves <- cost_curves |>
  left_join(panels, by = "k") |>
  mutate(panel = fct_inorder(panel))
at_cheapest <- semi_join(cost_curves, cheapest,
                         by = c("k", "threshold" = "cheapest threshold"))
without_model <- left_join(cheapest, panels, by = "k")

ggplot(cost_curves, aes(threshold, cost, colour = panel)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(data = without_model, aes(yintercept = `cost without the model`),
             colour = "grey45", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = at_cheapest, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_ml() +
  labs(x = "Threshold", y = "Expected cost\n(misses per station)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

:::

The cheapest thresholds are `r f2(cost_of(1, "cheapest threshold"))`,
`r f2(cost_of(3, "cheapest threshold"))` and `r f2(cost_of(5, "cheapest threshold"))`,
against `r f2(cost_of(1, "k / (1 + k)"))`, `r f2(cost_of(3, "k / (1 + k)"))` and
`r f2(cost_of(5, "k / (1 + k)"))` from the rule: logistic regression's probabilities are
calibrated well enough for the rule to work. When a false alarm costs five misses, the
cheapest threshold calls `r cost_of(5, "stations called present")` of the
`r nrow(survey)` stations present, and leaving the threshold at 0.5 costs
`r f2(cost_of(5, "cost at 0.5") / cost_of(5, "cost there"))` times as much. The model
is the same in every panel; only the threshold has changed.

The rules without a model are hard to beat here, because the species was caught at
`r pct(mean(present))` of the stations. At five to one, a threshold of 0.5 costs
`r f2(cost_of(5, "cost at 0.5"))` per station, more than the
`r f2(cost_of(5, "cost without the model"))` of calling no station present at all. The
cheapest threshold costs `r f2(cost_of(5, "cost there"))`, a saving of
`r pct(1 - cost_of(5, "cost there") / cost_of(5, "cost without the model"))` on that rule.
A model is worth using only at a threshold that suits the costs, and only if it beats the
rules that need none.

## The report states what the measure assumes

A measure carries assumptions, and the report should state them. A shortlist measure assumes
a budget, and the order of the models can change with it, so compute it at the budget the
survey really has. A threshold assumes a ratio of costs. Leaving it at 0.5 assumes that a
false alarm and a miss cost the same, which is rarely true and rarely written down. "Stations
above 0.75 were called present, as a wasted dive costs about three times a missed record" is
a sentence a reader can check, and one that lets someone with other costs reuse the model.

Every measure in this section compares predictions with what the survey recorded. If the
records themselves are biased, by the gear, the observers or where the effort went, a model
that matches them well matches the bias too, and no measure can show it.
[From a model to a claim](../10-interpretation/from-model-to-claim.qmd) shows such a gear
on the survey.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- Choose the measure from the use of the predictions, before fitting: a map, a total, a
  shortlist, a map of chances, or a call at each station.
- A **shortlist** is scored on the animals it finds, against a perfect and a random one. It
  depends only on the order of the predictions: the forest on log counts predicted
  `r pct(list_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` of the catch, yet its shortlist of
  `r budget` stations found about as many animals as the other models'.
- The **expected cost** of the calls counts misses and false alarms by what each costs. If a
  false alarm costs $k$ misses, calibrated probabilities are cheapest at a threshold of
  $k/(1+k)$.
- For logistic regression the cheapest thresholds fell at
  `r f2(cost_of(1, "cheapest threshold"))`, `r f2(cost_of(3, "cheapest threshold"))` and
  `r f2(cost_of(5, "cheapest threshold"))`. At five to one, a threshold of 0.5 cost more
  than calling no station present at all.
- State the budget and the cost ratio behind a measure. A threshold of 0.5 assumes the two
  mistakes cost the same.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Work out the shortlists for budgets of 50 and 200 stations. Does the same model find the
   most animals at every budget?
2. Use the random forest's probabilities of presence from
   [Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd) in place of logistic
   regression's. Do the cheapest thresholds still fall at $k/(1+k)$?
